19717-the-bostonians-vol-i-of-ii:
Henry James published The Bostonians in 1886, and it remains among his sharpest American novels. Volume one of two opens with a Southern visitor arriving in Boston. A lady in the scene teases him about being a Southerner. Olive Chancellor, the hostess, has sent word hoping he will stay to dinner. The visitor is her cousin, Basil Ransom, a Mississippian lawyer in New York.

James pits Ransom against Olive for the future of a young speaker, Verena Tarrant. Reform-era Boston, with its causes and drawing rooms, fills the stage. The novel's real fight is over ideas, charm, and control. James tells it in dense, ironic prose. Volume one sets the triangle that volume two will tighten.
20102-the-international-monthly-magazine:
The International Monthly Magazine, volume five, number two, gathers essays and reviews for its readers. One piece weighs the fame of a famed general of the Peninsula War. It grants him rare skill in many fields of command. Yet it denies him the first rank among great generals of history.

That fame, it argues, rests much on Napier's glowing history of the war. Napier wrote with skill but also with clear bias, the essay says. Monthly magazines then served as courts for such debates on fame. Readers get a sharp sample of 1850s literary and military argument.
20300-henry-viii:
Henry VIII, in this biography, first appeared in June 1902 with many pictures. A new edition came in May 1905 from Longmans, Green and Company. It was reprinted in January 1913 and again in October 1919. Its author also wrote lives of Cranmer and of Protector Somerset.

Henry remains one of England's most debated and dramatic kings. Six wives, a broken church, and vast power mark his reign. A life of Henry must weigh charm against cruelty at each turn. Readers get a scholarly yet readable portrait from a seasoned Tudor historian. Later lives have judged him more harshly, but few match this one's steady learning.
20947-memoirs-of-the-jacobites-of-1715-a:
Royal favour, high missions, and rich marriages built one family's power in volume two. Memoirs of the Jacobites traces such houses across the risings of 1715 and 1745. Intermarriage with Scotland's richest, noblest lines swelled their sway by degrees.

More lives of Stuart loyalists fill this second volume of Thomson's set. Exile, plots, scaffolds, and stubborn hope mark their varied ends. Family papers give the tales their warmth and their proof. Together the volumes keep a whole lost cause in view, through the men and women who paid its price in full.
20948-memoirs-of-the-jacobites-of-1715-a:
Letters never before in print grace the life of the Earl of Kilmarnock in volume three. Family helpers aided the Derwentwater life with zeal and exact knowledge. Memoirs of the Jacobites closes its set with Charles Radcliffe's tale so aided.

Last lives of the 1745 rising's doomed circle fill the final volume. Kilmarnock and Radcliffe both faced the axe for their Stuart loyalty. Their letters show love, faith, and grit at the edge of death. Thomson's three volumes end as they began, keen to give the Jacobites their due from a fairer age.
22069-the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-vol:
Guy de Maupassant wrote more perfect short stories than any Frenchman of his century. This eighth volume of his collected works in English shows his range. It opens with his famous essay on the novel. After reading Manon Lescaut, Don Quixote, Werther, Clarissa, Candide, and Madame Bovary, he asks, what may a novelist still attempt? The essay answers with Maupassant's own creed of truth seen through one temperament.

Stories fill the rest of the volume in his clear, hard style. Peasants, clerks, soldiers, and Parisian lovers pass under his cold eye. Maupassant died at forty-two, leaving some three hundred tales. This volume, essay included, is a strong place to meet him.
22086-the-son-of-monte-cristo-volume-ii:
Volume II of The Son of Monte-Cristo carries the sequel to Dumas's great romance toward its end. Spero, the Count's son, sleeps while the household gathers in Fanfaro's dining room. Monte-Cristo, Albert de Morcerf, Miss Clary, and Madame Caraman are all present. They have come to hear Fanfaro tell the story of his adventures.

Fanfaro's tale fills the volume with escapes, disguises, and old scores settled. The younger generation must finish what the Count began. Love, honour, and vengeance pull the characters in opposite directions. Readers of the first volume get the promised payoff here, in the same high-coloured style that made the Monte Cristo sequel a popular success.
22477-wintry-peacock-from-the-new-decame:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Wintry Peacock for the third volume of the New Decameron. The scene places a man and woman among cart-shed shafts. The shed faces the road where they stand talking.

She looks down at the ground, a little sideways. A small black frown shows on her brows as she broods. Then she looks straight into his eyes without warning. He blinks and wants to turn his face aside. Her look was too near, he admits, searching him for something. The frown stays on her keen, sallow brow throughout. Lawrence builds the whole tale's tension from glances like these. Readers get his charged, spare storytelling at work.
22849-the-history-of-tasmania-volume-ii:
John West's History of Tasmania reaches back to 1643 in this second volume. At the era of Tasman's discovery, he writes, Van Diemen's Land was already inhabited. The Dutch heard voices and a trumpet-like sound, saw smoke from fires, and noticed notches cut five feet apart in tree bark. They guessed at giants or at some unusual way of climbing.

West builds his colonial history from such early encounters forward. Settlement, government, conflict, and the fate of the island's first people all enter the record. He wrote as a participant in the colony's public life, and his judgments carry that closeness. The volume remains a standard early source on Tasmania, valuable and open to question in the usual ways of pioneer history.
a-half-century-of-conflict-volume-ii:
Francis Parkman's history of the French and English struggle for North America reaches its second volume here, covering the years from 1697 into the 1750s. Parkman wrote with a novelist's pace and a scholar's appetite for documents, and the volume forms part of his larger France and England in North America series. Its ground is the whole continent, from the St. Lawrence to the Missouri and the Red River.

French explorers push west, La Vérendrye's family hunts for a route to the Pacific, and rival forts rise along the chain of posts. The war chapters give the siege and capture of Louisbourg in 1745, the wreck of the Duc d'Anville expedition, and the Acadian conflicts that followed. Readers get narrative history at full stretch, driven by men, missions, and forts competing for a continent.
a-theological-political-treatise-part-ii:
Baruch Spinoza argues about Scripture, faith, and reason in part three of his Theologico-Political Treatise, covering chapters eleven to fifteen. The contents list shows the topics plainly. One chapter asks whether the apostles wrote as prophets or as teachers. Another asks why Scripture is called sacred and the word of God.

Later chapters say Scripture teaches only simple doctrines needed for right conduct, define faith, and separate faith from philosophy once and for all. The last chapter argues that theology is not the servant of reason, nor reason of theology. Spinoza writes calmly, but his claims about free thought were bold and risky.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-ii:
The second tome of Barbier de Meynard's Les Prairies d'Or appeared in 1863. It continues his complete French rendering of the Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi, the tenth-century Arab traveler and historian of Baghdad. The full French set runs to nine tomes, printed for the Société Asiatique between 1861 and 1877.

Al-Masudi's book is a world in one work. It holds geography, the histories of the Persians, Greeks, Romans, and Jews, and the deeds of the caliphs down to his own day. He mixes what he read with what he saw on his travels to India and East Africa. Meynard's notes steady the reader through the names. This tome is one link in that whole.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-iii:
Tome three of the French Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi came out in 1864, in Barbier de Meynard's translation for the Société Asiatique. Al-Masudi, who died in 956, had traveled from Persia to East Africa and read the books of many peoples. His Meadows of Gold is part history, part geography, part cabinet of wonders.

Readers of the whole work meet creation lore, king lists, the marvels of India and China, and the long story of the caliphate. Al-Masudi loves a good tale and tells where he heard it. The French version, with Pavet de Courteille, is the complete one in a Western tongue. This volume holds one stretch of that great road.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-vii:
Barbier de Meynard published the seventh tome of Les Prairies d'Or in 1873. The book renders the Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi, the Arab historian and traveler who died in 956. His Meadows of Gold gathers all he had read and seen across a life of travel from Syria to Ceylon.

In the full work the reader moves from the creation through the kings of the earth to the caliphs of Islam. Geography, natural wonders, and court tales are woven through the annals. Al-Masudi is curious about everything and credulous about some of it, which is part of his charm. The French notes guide the way. Tome seven brings the end of the set in sight.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-viii:
The eighth tome of the French Muruj al-Dhahab came out in 1874, in Barbier de Meynard's version for the Société Asiatique. Al-Masudi, its tenth-century author, called his book the Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems. He meant it as a feast of history and geography drawn from his travels and his reading.

Kings of Persia and Rome, the prophets, the peoples of India and Africa, and the caliphs of Baghdad all pass through his pages. He pauses for pearls, earthquakes, singing sands, and the habits of strange birds. The French text, made with Pavet de Courteille, is the complete rendering in a Western language. One tome remains after this.
alcibiades-ii:
Benjamin Jowett translated this short dialogue, and his appendix states plainly that it is by an imitator of Plato, not by Plato himself. It likely comes from the second or third generation after Plato, when his style was widely copied. Socrates finds Alcibiades on his way to pray and asks what he means to request.

The talk shows that men often pray for things that would harm them, since they do not know what is truly good. Socrates praises an old prayer that asks the gods to give good things and withhold bad ones, whether asked or not. The piece is brief, but its puzzle about prayer still feels fresh, as Jowett's notes observe.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-ii:
Book II of Athens: Its Rise and Fall, by Edward Bulwer Lytton, runs from Solon's legislation to Marathon. Its heading dates the span 594 to 490 BC. Lytton begins with the symptom of crisis. The laws of Draco were unduly severe. That severity, he argues, proves a general discontent. Harsh law rarely confirms a government. It usually strengthens a people against it. Scarcely were they enacted when Cylon's conspiracy struck.

Cylon, an Olympic victor married to the tyrant of Megara's daughter, seized the citadel on an oracle's encouragement and failed. Then Solon appears, first in the struggle for Salamis against the Megarians, then as lawgiver. His legislation fills the book's center. The strange career of the Pisistratid tyrants follows. Marathon closes the arc. The citizen militia Solon's city bred defeats the empire that swallowed Ionia.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-iii:
Athens: Its Rise and Fall, Book III, by Edward Bulwer Lytton, appears at the head of his history's second volume. Its contents open with Miltiades after Marathon. His naval expedition and the siege of Paros follow. Accusation, sentence, and death in disgrace close his story. Lytton then pauses the politics for a full chapter on the Athenian tragedy, from Thespis and Phrynichus to an analysis of Aeschylus, the soldier poet of Marathon's generation.

Aristides and the rising Themistocles divide the next chapter. It covers the ostracism, the vote that exiled men by potsherd. It covers the silver mines of Laurion. Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend their product on a navy. Then Darius prepares and dies. Xerxes resolves on the conquest of Europe. Book III is the history's hinge. Athens becomes a sea power just in time to need one.
book-of-etiquette-volume-ii:
Lillian Eichler's Book of Etiquette, Volume Two, continues her popular guide to manners for American readers. The volume opens with a tea table, properly uncluttered, and proceeds through the household, the dinner table and the social calendar.

Part Three treats servants in detail: the butler, the second man, the chauffeur, the valet, the page, the lady's maid and the nurse-maid, with correct dress and duties for each. Later chapters plan the formal dinner, with the American hostess at the centre. Readers curious about how 1920s America taught itself good manners will find Eichler practical, confident and full of period detail.
cameos-from-english-history-from-rollo-t: Cameos from English History, from Rollo to Edward II, by Charlotte Yonge. The historical sketches. This book preserves that history. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abstemii:
An abstemius cannot take wine without risking vomiting. Since Mass consecration requires both species, bread and wine, such a person is consequently irregular. St. Alphonsus, following Francisco Suarez, teaches that this irregularity is of divine law, so no papal dispensation covers it. The term also covers one with a strong distaste for wine who can still take a little.

That distaste alone is not irregularity, but a papal dispensation is needed to excuse wine at the chalice purification and finger ablutions. A decree of Propaganda from 13 January 1665 granted such a dispensation to missionaries in China, where wine was scarce. Heretics also imposed wine abstention at times, and Tatian's Encratites used water even in the sacrament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-ii:
Albert II, or Albrecht II, was the eighteenth Archbishop of Magdeburg in Saxony, the son of Gunther III, Count of Kevernburg, who died in 1232. He studied at Hildesheim, Paris, and Bologna and became a prebendary of Magdeburg cathedral young. He was consecrated bishop by the pope at Rome in December 1206. He entered Magdeburg on Palm Sunday in April 1207, and five days later fire destroyed much of the city, including his cathedral.

Albert laid the foundation stone of today's cathedral in 1208 and rebuilt much of the city, earning credit as founder of the Neustadt, the new town. He brought the Dominicans to Magdeburg in 1224 and the Franciscans in 1225, and founded a women's convent honouring St. Mary Magdalen. Beyond his diocese he played a leading part in the struggle for the imperial crown, shifting his support from Otto IV to Frederick II after Otto's excommunication in 1211.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalricus-aug:
Amalricus Augerii was a fourteenth-century church historian and Augustinian, doctor of the University of Montpellier, prior of a monastery of his order, and chaplain to Urban V in 1362. His learning was great, above all in church history. His offices joined scholarship, monastic rule, and papal court service in one varied career.

His chief work, Actus Romanorum Pontificum, runs alphabetically from St. Peter to 1321, edited chronologically in Eccard's Scriptores medii aevi, volume two, pages 1641 to 1824. An alphabetical pontifical history to 1321, it orders the popes for ready reference rather than narrative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anacletus-ii:
Anacletus II was the title taken by Cardinal Pietro Pierleone at the contested papal election of 1130, and he held it until his death on 25 January 1138. The Pierleoni ranked among the wealthiest and most powerful senatorial families of Rome, though men never forgot their Jewish descent or their rise through moneylending. Pierleone studied at Paris, became a monk at Cluny, and rose to cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Most cardinals and nearly all the people of Rome stood behind him, and his rival Innocent fled the city. Yet Bernard of Clairvaux won nearly the whole Christian world for Innocent, judging his election purer, more regular, and earlier, and his character above attack. When Anacletus died, Rome preferred Innocent so plainly that his successor Victor IV soon submitted, ending an eight-year schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipope-john:
Antipope 997-998, died probably in 1013. After John XV's death, Bruno, Otto III's chaplain, became Gregory V, crowned May 996. In May the new pope crowned young Otto III emperor in Rome. After Otto left, Crescentius drove the pope from Rome in September 996. In May 997 Crescentius made Archbishop John Philagathus antipope, fresh from a Constantinople mission. John was a Rossano, Calabria, native, then Byzantine territory.

St. Nilus, John's compatriot, vainly dissuaded him. At Pavia's 997 synod Gregory V excommunicated Crescentius. That winter Otto III entered Rome in February 998; the antipope fled, Crescentius held Sant' Angelo. John was captured, blinded, nose and ears mutilated, and brought to Rome. Gregory V deposed him; at Nilus's plea he went from prison to a monastery. At Easter 998 Otto took Sant' Angelo; Crescentius was beheaded. The Annales Fuldenses date John's death 2 April 1013.

Pisan antipope, born about 1370, died November 1419. Cossa was among seven cardinals deserting Gregory XII in May 1408 to convene Pisa's council, which he led. Of an impoverished Neapolitan noble family, he took arms in youth, later forsaking them for the Church. Energetic and talented, he took a Bologna law degree and entered the curia. In 1402 Boniface IX made him cardinal; next year he became legate of Romandiola.

A 1412 Roman council drew so few it was prorogued repeatedly, condemning only Wycliff before dissolving in March 1413. In May 1413 Ladislaus invaded Rome's province; John fled to Florence, seeking a general council to end the schism. Deposed at Constance in May 1415, John submitted. Secular and ambitious, his morals not above reproach, yet his foes exaggerated gravely. As Cossa again, he was confined at Rudolfzell, Gottlieben, Heidelberg, and Mannheim until Martin V's election freed him in 1418; he did homage to Martin V at Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolici-mi:
Apostolici Ministerii is a bull of Innocent XIII, dated 23 May 1724, aimed at reviving church discipline in Spain. The primate, or chief bishop, and King Philip had reported that the Council of Trent's disciplinary laws were gradually falling out of use. The pope sent the matter before the Sacred Congregation of the Council and, on its advice, issued the bull, laying down rules for secular and regular clergy in Spain.

Leading points include tonsure, the first clerical rite, granted only where religion demands it, with each cleric assigned to a church. Seminarians attend the cathedral on feast days only, so study is not broken. Candidates for orders must be examined and shown to know enough. Ordination titles, or incomes, must be sufficient for decent support, and shaky benefices are suppressed. Priests with care of souls must also teach their flocks regularly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-xii:
Benedict XII, born Jacques Fournier, was the third pope to rule from Avignon, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born at Saverdun in France, he was elected in December 1334 and died at Avignon in 1342. A Cistercian monk and Paris-trained theologian, he rose through Fontfroide abbey and the bishoprics of Pamiers and Mirepoix before his election.

Reform was his chief concern. He sent absentee clergy back to their posts, revoked his predecessors' promised appointments, and attacked plural holding of church offices. He stayed at Avignon despite hopes of return to Rome, and in 1339 began building the great papal palace that still stands. Money for famine relief in Italy and for church repair shows the other side of his rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benno-ii:
Benno II, bishop of Osnabrück, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Lünigen in Swabia, he died in 1088 at the monastery of Iburg near Osnabrück. Schooled at Strasbourg under the learned Hermann of Reichenau, he taught at Speyer after a pilgrimage to the Holy Land.

Skill in building made him imperial architect to Emperor Henry III, overseeing castles and churches across the empire. When the Rhine threatened Speyer cathedral, Benno's engineering saved its foundations. Later, as bishop, he long sided with Emperor Henry IV against Pope Gregory VII. He signed the deposition of 1076, was freed from excommunication at Canossa, and retired to Iburg, the monastery he had founded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-iii:
Boniface III, pope for less than a year in 607, won from Emperor Phocas the decree that Rome heads all churches. A Roman deacon and son of John Cataadioce, he served Gregory the Great as legate at Constantinople from 603, winning Phocas's regard by tact and prudence. After a near-year vacancy he was consecrated on 19 February 607 and died on 12 November.

His decree against Cyriacus of Constantinople reserved the title Universal Bishop to Rome alone. At Rome he held a council of the Roman clergy with seventy-two bishops, forbidding any discussion of a successor during a pope's or bishop's lifetime. No steps for a successor could begin until three days after burial. The council's acts are lost, and he was buried in Saint Peter's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-vii:
Boniface VII, born Franco, was an intruder pope whose two seizures of Rome ended in murder and mob vengeance. In June 974, after Crescentius stirred revolt, Romans jailed Benedict VI in Sant'Angelo and raised Franco in his place. The imprisoned pope was soon put to death. Within little more than a month, Count Sicco retook the city, and Boniface fled to Constantinople with the Vatican treasury.

After nine years of exile, he returned on Otto II's death in 983, seized John XIV in April 984, and jailed him in Sant'Angelo, where John died four months later. Rome endured him for over a year. After his sudden death in July 985, probably by violence, his corpse was dragged through the streets and flung beneath the statue of Marcus Aurelius before clerics buried it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eanbald-ii: This 1913 reference article on Eanbald II — the Archbishop of York. George Hind notes his ninth-century reign. The entry preserves his modest fame. His see served the Danish age. A prelate of the Saxon Church. His 796 consecration is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-iii: This 1913 reference article on Edward III — the victor of Crécy. Thomas Williams unfolds his glorious reign. His archers swept the French chivalry. Windsor knew its chivalrous king. The founder of the Order of the Garter. His 1348 Garter is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugenius-ii: A 1913 entry on Eugenius II — the ninth-century pope. Mark McNeal notes his brief reign. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pontificate served the Carolingian age. A pope of the ninth century. His 824 pontificate is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-ii: This 1913 reference piece on Felix II — the fourth-century antipope. Johann Peter Kirsch unfolds his contested reign. The Arians raised the rival pontiff. The Church kept the lawful line. The schism of the Arian party. His 355 intrusion is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-ii: This 1913 reference article on Ferdinand II — the emperor of the Thirty Years' war. Karl Klaar unfolds his fateful reign. His edicts fired the German strife. Wallenstein served the imperial cause. The master of the Catholic restoration. His 1629 Edict is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fossombrone-f: A 1913 entry on Fossombrone — Forum Sempronii, the Marche diocese. Umberto Benigni gives its ancient story. Its bishops serve the Metauro's flock. The Furlo gorge guards the old town. A see of the Apennine valley. Its 5th-century see is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-ii: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Frederick II — the stupor mundi. Franz Kampers unfolds his wondrous reign. He defied the papal thunders. Sicily knew its learned king. The wonder of the medieval world. His 1250 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gennadius-ii: A 1913 entry on Gennadius II — the first Ottoman patriarch. Adrian Fortescue unfolds his fateful reign. He bowed to the conquering sultan. The Greeks kept the humbled throne. The Scholarius of the fallen empire. His 1473 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-iii: A 1913 entry on Henry III — the Salian emperor. Franz Kampers unfolds his mighty reign. He humbled the papal throne. The empire knew the fearless lord. The master of the eleventh-century Reich. His 1056 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-viii: This 1913 reference piece on Henry VIII — the Tudor king. Herbert Thurston unfolds his schism's tale. He rent the English Church. The martyrs bled in his reign. The founder of the royal supremacy. His 1547 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-ii: This 1913 reference article on Joseph II — the enlightened emperor. Hermann Franz unfolds his fateful reforms. His edicts curbed the cloistered orders. The empire knew the restless name. The eighteenth century told his tale. His 1790 death is famed. His 1781 edicts are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-iii: A 1913 entry on Julius III — the Renaissance pope. Michael Ott unfolds his troubled reign. He faced the reforming storm. Rome knew the courtly name. The sixteenth century told his tale. His 1555 death is famed. His 1550 reign is famed. His 1550 Villa Giulia is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jus-spolii: A 1913 entry on Jus Spolii — the spoil right. Andrew Meehan unfolds its canonical lore. It seized the dead prelate's goods. The canonists weighed the seemly bounds. The Church kept its ancient use. Its medieval practice is famed. Its 1910 study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lamp-and-lamp: This 1913 reference piece on Lamps and Lampadarii — the sanctuary lights. Herbert Thurston unfolds their ritual lore. The flames guard the sacred host. The Church keeps the ancient use. The altars know their glow. Their sanctuary flames are famed. Their 1907 study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leo-vii: This 1913 reference article on Leo VII — the Cluniac pope. Horace Mann notes his brief reign. His rule crowned the tenth century. Rome knew the holy name. The entry keeps its modest fame. His 939 death is famed. His 936 reign is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leo-viii: A 1913 entry on Leo VIII — the disputed pope. Horace Mann unfolds his tangled tale. He faced the rival's claims. Rome knew the stormy name. The tenth century told his story. His 965 death is famed. His 963 election is famed. His 963 Roman schism is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-napoleon-iii: Napoleon III built the Second Empire on his uncle's name, protected the pope's temporal power until 1870, then lost everything at Sedan. This entry covers his reign, his Catholic policy, and his collapse. The little nephew with the great name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-ii: Otto II, the Red, ruled the empire from 973 to 983 and dreamed of uniting East and West. This entry covers his reign, his wars in Italy, and his early death. The emperor who reached too far: his southern dream died at Crotone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-iii: Otto III was the wonder-child emperor who dreamed of a renewed Rome with Pope Sylvester II. This entry covers his reign, his visions, and his death at twenty-one. The emperor of the year 1000: his renovatio dreamed of a Christian world-empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paschal-iii: Paschal III was the antipope set up by Barbarossa against Alexander III in 1164. This entry traces his schism, his imperial backing, and his failure. The emperor's pope: his brief schism divided all of Germany for a whole troubled decade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelagius-ii: Pelagius II was the pope who raised Gregory the Great and faced the Lombard invasions. This entry covers his pontificate, his letters, and his times. Gregory's master on Peter's throne: his surviving letters reveal a deeply troubled and embattled pontificate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-ii: Philip Augustus was the French king who humbled England's Plantagenets and built Paris. This entry traces his reign, his victories, and his administration. The maker of medieval France: his glorious Bouvines victory crowned his long and triumphant reign over France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-adrian-i: Adrian II was the pope of the Photian schism's crisis and the eighth ecumenical council. This entry traces his pontificate, his trials, and his letters. The pope of the stormy 870s: his brave legates faced the proud Eastern schism unflinching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-agapetus: Agapetus II was the pope of the iron 900s, ruling Rome amid the nobles' feuds. This entry traces his pontificate, his privileges, and his times. The pope of the saeculum obscurum: his generous grants favored great Cluny's mighty rise to power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-alexande: Alexander II was the pope who blessed the Gregorian reform and the Normans' England. This entry traces his pontificate, his legates, and his battles. The pope of Hildebrand's shadow: his blessed banner flew at bloody Hastings in 1066 for William.

Alexander III was the pope who faced Barbarossa and canonized Becket. This entry traces his long pontificate, his exiles, and his triumphs. The lawyer-pope of the twelfth century: his learned decrees shaped all medieval canon law forever and ever afterward.

Alexander VII was the Chigi pope of Bernini's colonnade and the Jansenist storm. This entry traces his pontificate, his art, and his diplomacy. The connoisseur on Peter's throne: his vast colonnade embraces St. Peter's square today in white travertine stone.

Alexander VIII was the Ottoboni pope whose brief reign enriched his nephews. This entry traces his pontificate, his nepotism, and his times. The pope of the last great nepotism: his grasping Ottoboni kin filled the whole Roman Curia with nephews.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-anastasi: Anastasius II was the pope of 496 whose dealings with Constantinople bred legend. This entry traces his pontificate, his letters, and the Dantean myth. The pope Dante placed in hell: his misleading tomb inscription bred the unjust legend of heresy.

Anastasius III was the pope of the early 900s, a quiet name in a dark age. This entry notes his brief pontificate and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. A shadow on Peter's throne: his two years left barely a trace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict: Benedict III was the pope whose election the emperor tried to overturn. This entry traces his pontificate, his trials, and his vindication. The pope of the imperial intrusion: his holy election defied the emperor Louis II himself in imperial Rome.

Benedict VII was the pope of the late 900s who curbed the Roman nobles. This entry notes his pontificate, his synods, and his reforms. The reformer before the reform: his reforming synods curbed the Roman simoniacs and usurers alike at Rome.

Benedict VIII was the warrior pope who crushed the Saracens at Ostia. This entry traces his pontificate, his battles, and his reforms. The Tusculan on the throne: his Christian fleet broke the Saracen pirates at sea near Ostia in 1016.

Benedict XIII was the saintly Orsini pope, austere amid the baroque. This entry traces his pontificate, his reforms, and his holiness. The ascetic of the eighteenth century: his secret hair shirt shamed the silk-clad courtiers around him daily in Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-bl-urban: Urban II was the pope who launched the First Crusade at Clermont. This entry traces his pontificate, his preaching, and his triumph. The pope of Deus vult: his fiery call freed holy Jerusalem from the infidel at last in 1099.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-blessed-: Eugene III was the Cistercian pope, St. Bernard's disciple on the throne. This entry traces his pontificate, his exiles, and his holiness. The monk who became pope: his great master Bernard guided his troubled reign from far Clairvaux Abbey in France.

Victor III was the blessed abbot of Monte Cassino who reluctantly became pope. This entry traces his pontificate, his abbacy, and his sanctity. Desiderius on Peter's throne: his glorious abbey was all Christendom's wonder and pride in gleaming stone and gold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-boniface: Boniface II was the Ostrogothic pope of the 530s, first of the Germanic line. This entry notes his pontificate, his decrees, and the scant records. The Goth on Peter's throne: his contested election split the Roman clergy in two rival camps.

Boniface VIII was the pope of Unam Sanctam and the outrage of Anagni. This entry traces his pontificate, his clash with Philip the Fair, and his fall. The last of the medieval theocrats: his Jubilee of 1300 drew Rome's crowds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-callistu: Callistus II was the pope of the Concordat of Worms, ending the Investiture Contest. This entry traces his pontificate, his Lateran council, and his triumph. The peacemaker of Church and empire: his great council crowned the long Gregorian reform triumphantly.

Callistus III was the first Borgia pope, who ordered Joan of Arc's retrial. This entry traces his pontificate, his crusade plans, and his nepotism. The Valencian on the throne: his papal fleet fought the advancing Turk at sea in vain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-celestin: Celestine II was the pope of 1143 whose brief reign soothed the schism's wounds. This entry notes his pontificate and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. A quiet name of the twelfth century: his months soothed the schism.

Celestine III was the aged pope of the 1190s who crowned Henry VI. This entry traces his pontificate, his letters, and his diplomacy. The nonagenarian of the twelfth century: his long life spanned the great crusades of olden days gone by.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-: Clement II was the German reform pope crowned by Henry III. This entry traces his pontificate, his synods, and his sudden death. The Bamberg bishop on the throne: his bold reform synods shook proud imperial Rome itself awake at last.

Clement III was the pope of the 1180s who made peace with the Romans. This entry traces his pontificate, his return to Rome, and his letters. The peacemaker of the Capitol: his triumphant return ended the long Roman exile at last.

Clement VII was the Medici pope of the Sack of Rome and Henry's divorce. This entry traces his pontificate, his disasters, and his diplomacy. The unluckiest of the Renaissance popes: his beloved Rome burned in the cruel sack of 1527.

Clement VIII was the Aldobrandini pope who absolved Henry IV. This entry traces his pontificate, his jubilee, and his statesmanship. The pope of the French absolution: his great jubilee drew the Catholic nations to holy Rome in the crowds of 1600.

Clement XII was the blind Corsini pope who built the Trevi fountain's age. This entry traces his pontificate, his buildings, and his reforms. The builder of the Lateran facade: his great fountain sings in baroque Rome today for all to hear.

Clement XIII was the Rezzonico pope who defended the Jesuits to his death. This entry traces his pontificate, his courage, and the suppression storm. The protector of the Society: his brave brief defended the persecuted Jesuits of all Catholic Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-damasus-: Damasus II was the pope whose reign lasted twenty-three days in 1048. This entry notes his German origin, his brief days, and his death. The pope of three weeks: his early death doomed the young reform's hope in Germany forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-eugene-i: Eugene II was the pope of the 820s who crowned Lothair's son. This entry notes his pontificate, his synods, and the scant records. A quiet name of the Carolingian age: his reforming synods ordered the lax Roman clergy strictly and well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gelasius: Gelasius II was the pope who fled Henry V and died in exile at Cluny. This entry traces his pontificate, his flight, and his death. The fugitive pope of 1119: his sad exile ended at great Cluny's abbey in Burgundy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-: Gregory VIII was the pope of two months whose crusade call shook Christendom. This entry traces his brief pontificate and the fall of Jerusalem's news. The pope of Audita Tremendi: his dying call launched the great Third Crusade of kings.

Gregory XII was the pope who resigned to end the Great Schism. This entry traces his pontificate, his abdication, and his lonely end. The pope who gave up the tiara: his lonely sacrifice ended the long schism at Constance's council.

Gregory XIII was the pope of the calendar that bears his name. This entry traces his pontificate, his reform, and his colleges. The pope of the new calendar: his bold reform dropped ten autumn days in 1582's October overnight by decree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-honorius: Honorius II was the pope of the 1120s who approved the Templars' rule. This entry traces his pontificate, his crusade plans, and his letters. The pope of the white mantles: his solemn approval armed the new Templars for holy war.

Honorius III was the gentle pope who approved Francis and Dominic. This entry traces his pontificate, his bulls, and his crusade. The pope of the two great founders: his gentle bulls blessed the preaching friars of holy God forever in love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent: Innocent II was the pope who triumphed over the antipope Anacletus. This entry traces his pontificate, his exiles, and his Lateran council. The victor of the double election: his Lateran council crowned the hard triumph of 1139's bright spring in Rome.

Innocent III was the greatest pope of the Middle Ages, master of kings. This long entry traces his pontificate, his crusades, and his Lateran council. The apex of the papal monarchy: his dread interdicts humbled mighty kings and proud emperors.

Innocent VII was the pope of the Roman obedience's troubled years. This entry traces his pontificate, his flight, and his return. The pope of the schism's storms: his timely flight saved the Roman obedience from utter ruin in 1408's flight.

Innocent VIII was the Cybo pope of the late 1400s, first to acknowledge his children. This entry traces his pontificate, his nepotism, and his times. The pope of the witches' bull: his dark Summis Desiderantes armed the witch hunters of Germany.

Innocent XII was the pope who forever banned papal nepotism. This entry traces his pontificate, his bull Romanum Decet, and his reforms. The ender of the nephews' age: his solemn bull forbade the shameful practice forevermore in 1692's famous decree.

Innocent XIII was the Conti pope of the early 1720s. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his conclave's drama, and the scant records. A quiet name of the eighteenth century: his deadlocked conclave lasted weary months in 1721's bright spring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-ii: John II was the first pope to change his name, dropping the pagan Mercurius. This entry traces his pontificate, his decrees, and his precedent. The pope who chose a new name: his wise precedent guides every conclave since that day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-iii: John III was the pope of the Lombard invasions who fled to the catacombs. This entry notes his pontificate, his exile, and the scant records. The pope of the underground months: his prudent flight saved the papacy itself from ruin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-vii: John VII was the Greek pope whose mosaics adorn Santa Maria Antiqua. This entry traces his pontificate, his art, and his timidity. The artist pope of the Forum: his bright mosaics glow in the ancient ruins of the Roman Forum.

John VIII was the pope murdered by his own household after defending Rome. This entry traces his pontificate, his Saracen wars, and his assassination. The first murdered pope: his treacherous killers struck in 882's dark December night by poison and hammer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xii: John XII was the boy-pope Octavian whom Otto the Great deposed. This entry traces his pontificate, his scandals, and his fall. The most dissolute of the medieval popes: his Roman synod deposed him in 963's cold winter months at Rome.

John XIII was the pope whom the Romans expelled and Otto restored. This entry traces his pontificate, his exile, and his triumph. The pope of the imperial restoration: his holy crown graced young Otto's son in 967's bright Christmas morning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xvi: This entry covers the brief pontificates of John XVII and John XVIII at the millennium's turn. It traces their reigns and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. Two shadows of the year 1000: their months barely troubled history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xxi: John XXII was the Avignon pope of the poverty controversy and the long reign. This entry traces his pontificate, his battles with the Franciscans, and his canonizations. The banker-pope of Avignon: his vast treasury funded the Italian wars for decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-julius-i: Julius II was the warrior pope who commissioned Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling. This long entry traces his pontificate, his wars, and his art. The terrible pope of the Renaissance: his warlike beard defied the French king himself in open war for Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-xii: Leo XII was the della Genga pope of the Holy Year 1825. This entry traces his pontificate, his jubilee, and his conservatism. The ascetic of the Restoration age: his stern austerity shamed the luxurious Roman court of the old regime.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-xiii: Leo XIII was the pope of Rerum Novarum and the workingman's charter. This long entry traces his pontificate, his encyclicals, and his diplomacy. The wisest pope of the modern age: his noble Thomism renewed the Catholic schools worldwide in faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-lucius-i: Lucius II was the pope killed by a stone at the Capitol in 1145. This entry traces his brief pontificate, his war with the Romans, and his death. The pope of the commune's stones: his violent death doomed the republic.

Lucius III was the pope who condemned the Waldensians at Verona. This entry traces his pontificate, his decrees, and his exile. The pope of Ad Abolendam: his stern decree outlawed the heretics of Lombardy and of far southern Languedoc forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-marcellu: Marcellus II was the pope whose reign lasted twenty-two days in 1555. This entry traces his election, his reforming hopes, and his death. The pope of Palestrina's Mass: his holy name graces the immortal polyphony of eternal Rome forevermore in song.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-marinus-: Marinus II was the pope of the mid-940s, a quiet name in a dark age. This entry notes his pontificate and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. A shadow of the tenth century: his reign passed in silence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-nicholas: Nicholas II was the pope whose decree gave the cardinals the papal election. This entry traces his pontificate, his Lateran synod, and his reform. The founder of the conclave's law: his wise decree endures to this very day in force.

Nicholas III was the Orsini pope whom Dante punished for nepotism. This entry traces his pontificate, his kin, and his building. The pope of the Orsini triumph: his grasping kin ruled the whole Roman Curia outright and openly in power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paschal-: Paschal II was the pope humiliated by Henry V at St. Peter's. This entry traces his pontificate, his capture, and his concessions. The pope of the forced privilege: his abject surrender shamed the Gregorian reform forever in 1111's dark April.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-ii: Paul II was the Barbo pope who persecuted the humanists and loved jewels. This entry traces his pontificate, his splendor, and his feuds. The magnificent enemy of the academy: his jeweled tiara outshone the visiting kings themselves in barbaric splendor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-iii: Paul III was the Farnese pope who opened Trent and approved the Jesuits. This long entry traces his pontificate, his council, and his nepotism. The pope of the Counter-Reformation's dawn: his founding bulls armed the newborn Jesuits for spiritual battle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-ii: Pius II was the humanist Piccolomini pope who died crusading at Ancona. This long entry traces his pontificate, his Commentaries, and his dream. The scholar who would save Constantinople: his lonely death doomed the dreamed crusade at Ancona's lonely shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-iii: Pius III was the Piccolomini pope whose reign lasted twenty-six days. This entry traces his election, his hopes, and his death. The pope of a single autumn: his bright hopes died with him in 1503's brief autumn of bright promise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-vii: Pius VII was the pope who excommunicated Napoleon and crowned him. This long entry traces his pontificate, his captivity, and his restoration. The pope of the Napoleonic storm: his triumphant return thrilled all of Christian Europe in 1814's bright spring.

Pius VIII was the Castiglioni pope of the brief 1829 reign. This entry notes his pontificate, his encyclical, and his sudden death. The pope of seventeen months: his sudden death stunned the Roman conclave of 1830's cold winter months entirely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-le: Leo II was the saintly pope of 682 who confirmed Constantinople III. This entry notes his brief pontificate and his sanctity. The confirmer of the Sixth Council: his brief reign sealed the orthodox faith forever in 683's bright June days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sergius-: Sergius II was the pope whose Rome the Saracens sacked in 846. This entry traces his pontificate, the raid, and his rebuilding. The pope of the violated basilicas: his urgent rebuilding raised the Vatican walls anew in solid Roman stone.

Sergius III was the pope of the Theophylact age's darkest scandals. This entry traces his pontificate, his crimes, and the legends about him. The pope of the pornocracy's height: his violent reign stained the dark tenth century forever in blood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-adria: Adrian III was the saintly pope of 884 whose year ended on a Roman road. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his journey, and his sanctity. The pilgrim pope who died walking: his weary body rests at Nonantola's abbey in peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-bened: Benedict II was the saintly pope of the 680s, learned and gentle. This entry notes his pontificate, his charity, and his sanctity. The scholar-saint of the seventh century: his deep learning lit the Roman schools of olden days gone by.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-felix: Felix III was the saintly pope of the Acacian schism's long breach. This entry traces his pontificate, his excommunication of Acacius, and his sanctity. The pope of the thirty-five years' schism: his solemn anathema stood firm for decades unbroken in pride.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-grego: Gregory II was the saintly pope who defied the iconoclast emperor and sent Boniface north. This entry traces his pontificate, his courage, and his sanctity. The pope of the German mission's birth: his apostolic blessing sent Boniface northward to Germany.

Gregory III was the saintly Syrian pope who defied the iconoclasts. This entry traces his pontificate, his courage, and his sanctity. The last Eastern pope for twelve centuries: his holy icons defied the iconoclast emperor Leo the Isaurian himself in Rome.

Gregory VII was Hildebrand, the saint of Canossa and the reform's soul. This long entry traces his pontificate, his war with Henry IV, and his death in exile. The mightiest reformer of the papacy: his stern Dictatus shook the kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-leo-i: Leo III was the pope who crowned Charlemagne on Christmas night. This entry traces his pontificate, his attack, and his empire-making. The maker of the Holy Roman Empire: his Christmas crown made the medieval ages themselves in 800's holy December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-sixtu: Sixtus II was the saintly pope beheaded with his deacons in 258. This entry traces his pontificate, his martyrdom, and Lawrence's grief. The martyr of Valerian's edict: his brave deacons died around him in 258's bright August morning of martyrdom.

Sixtus III was the saintly pope who built Santa Maria Maggiore for the Theotokos. This entry traces his pontificate, his basilica, and his sanctity. The builder of the snow church: his apse mosaics blaze with heavenly gold today in Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-: Stephen II was the pope who crossed the Alps to crown Pepin. This entry traces his pontificate, the Donation, and his triumph. The pope of the Frankish alliance's birth: his holy anointing made a lasting Frankish dynasty at Soissons in 751.

This entry untangles the numbering of Stephen II, who died before consecration, and Stephen III. A specialized study of papal chronology as the 1913 editors recorded it, clarifying the ancient miscount for modern readers at very long last indeed in print.

Stephen VII was the pope strangled in prison in 931. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his fall, and the scant records. The murdered pope of the dark century: his secret stranglers left no name in history's dark pages at all.

Stephen VII was the pope of the mid-920s, a quiet name in a dark age. This entry notes his pontificate and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. A shadow of the tenth century: his reign passed in silence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sylveste: Sylvester II was Gerbert, the scholar-pope of the year 1000. This entry traces his pontificate, his science, and the magician legends. The wizard pope of the millennium: his strange astrolabe awed the fearful Romans of 1000's bright Easter morning at Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-theodore: Theodore II was the pope whose reign lasted twenty days in 897. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his rehabilitation of Formosus, and his death. The pope of three weeks' justice: his swift mercy restored the wronged dead to honor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-urban-ii: Urban III was the pope of the 1180s who died at the news of Hattin. This entry traces his brief pontificate, his crusade grief, and his death. The pope whom Hattin killed: his holy grief ended his brief reign in 1187.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-urban-vi: Urban VII was the pope whose reign lasted thirteen days in 1590. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his smoking ban, and his death. The pope of twelve days: his stern ban outlawed tobacco in all churches and churchyards forever.

Urban VIII was the Barberini pope of Galileo's trial and Bernini's bronze. This long entry traces his pontificate, his splendor, and his nepotism. The pope of the bees' reign: his seized bronze stripped the ancient Pantheon's noble portico for cannon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-victor-i: Victor II was the German reform pope, Gebhard of Eichstätt. This entry traces his brief pontificate, his regency, and his death. The emperor's pope of the reform: his wise regency ruled the German empire well and justly for young Henry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-vii: Raymond VII of Toulouse was the last count of the crusade's ruin. This entry traces his submission, his treaty, and his death. The penitent of Paris: his humbling treaty ended the Albigensian wars in 1229's fateful spring of peace in Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-referendarii: The Referendarii were the papal officials of petitions. This entry explains their office, their ranks, and their history. The referees of the Curia: their red seals sped the papal petitions of Europe's faithful in Rome's courts of grace and favor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regionarii: The Regionarii were the deacons of Rome's regions. This entry explains their office, their districts, and their history. The deacons of the seven hills: their seven regions served the Roman poor in charity and love and alms and prayer and song.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sandwich-isla: The Sandwich Islands became the vicariate of Hawaii. This entry covers its missionaries, its parishes, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Pacific kingdom: its stone cathedral crowns Honolulu in Oahu's town in the Pacific's isles of the kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anselm-duk: St. Anselm the Duke was the Lombard turned monk. This entry traces his Forum Julii, his Nonantola, and his cult. The prince of the Emilian abbey: his monastic vow crowned Nonantola in the 750s' Lombardy in the abbey of the plain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ferdinand-: St. Ferdinand III was the king of Castile and Leon. This long entry examines his reconquest, his Seville, and his cult. The saint of the Spanish throne: his victorious sword crowned Seville in the 1240s' Andalusia in the south of the peninsula.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-henry-ii: St. Henry II was the emperor of the Germans. This long entry examines his Bamberg, his Cunegunda, and his cult. The saint of the imperial throne: his imperial crown sealed Bamberg in the 1000s' Franconia in the north of the duchy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paulinus-i: St. Paulinus II was the patriarch of Aquileia. This entry traces his Charlemagne, his writings, and his fame. The theologian of the Carolingian court: his great see crowned Aquileia in the 780s' Friuli in the east of the province in the Isonzo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suppression-o: The suppression was the fall of the English abbeys. This very long entry examines its Cromwell, its spoils, and its sorrow. The ruin of the Tudor monasteries: their rich spoils crowned the courtiers in the 1530s' dissolution in the Thames.
doe-osti-3012130-pulsed-magnet-power-sys: NSLS-II got pulsed magnets, and this DOE text covers the power systems. The pages detail the findings. The accelerator folks get their data. The magnets were pulsed. The data were accelerator. The facility was NSLS-II. The systems were power.
egyptian-tales-translated-from-the-papyr:
W. M. Flinders Petrie's Egyptian Tales, Second Series, translates stories of the Eighteenth to Nineteenth Dynasties. Petrie warns that these are not fairy tales in the usual sense, since they relate the doings of men and women who are human, at times all too human.

Supernatural elements, he explains, belong to the beliefs and motives of the people pictured, and most of what happens might occur today where ancient beliefs still hold. No being in the volume could properly be called a fairy. Tristram Ellis illustrates the tales. Readers who enjoyed the first series will find this second volume equally vivid and human.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-matthew:
Alexander Maclaren's Expositions of Holy Scripture: St. Matthew, Chapters Nine to Twenty-Eight, continues his sermon expositions of the Gospels. Maclaren treats each passage as a text for preaching, drawing out its devotional and moral meaning.

Expositions include Christ's Encouragements, Soul-Healing First, The Call of Matthew, The Touch of Faith, The Obscure Apostles, and Christ's Charge to His Heralds. Later pieces treat John's doubts, the friend of publicans and sinners, the rest giver, and the Pharisees' Sabbath. Readers who value Maclaren's preaching will find this volume, like its companions, clear, warm and richly applied.
freytag-pictures-of-german-life-xviiixix:
The concluding volume of Freytag's Pictures of German Life, in English, finishes the story of Germany in the 1700s and 1800s. From Enlightenment salons to the brink of national unification, the narrative follows one long making of modern life. Workshops, schools, and parliaments all change across its pages.

Freytag keeps his novelist's eye on character while commanding a historian's range of fact. Middle-class families rise; old orders adapt or vanish; cities swallow villages. The volume completes a four-part panorama that taught generations of Germans their own everyday past. Its sympathy for ordinary people stays its chief virtue. English readers receive the whole arc of the project in this and the companion volumes.
freytag-pictures-of-german-life-xvxvii-c:
Volume Two of Freytag's Pictures of German Life, in English, completes his panorama of the fifteenth through seventeenth centuries. Trade routes, craft guilds, and family customs share pages with the wars of religion. Luther's age and its long aftermath receive the closest attention in this concluding half.

Freytag follows households through plague, inflation, and invasion with a storyteller's patience. The detail is a treasure house: how people dressed, worshipped, bargained, and buried their dead. A novelist's gifts keep the material breathing rather than dusty. Together the two volumes taught German readers to see their own past in daily things. English readers gain the same education in translation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_climate-:
Rachel Santarsiero edited this briefing book, number 905, published on September 30, 2025. It is the second part of a series on climate information vanishing from United States government sources. Its subject is a White House effort to remove and change data about climate change.

Outside organizations, the posting reports, were working to rescue climate data before it disappeared for good. The record connects that removal effort to distorted science and to deregulation. It documents a fight over public information itself: who controls the numbers that climate policy depends on, and what happens when they are taken down.
king-edward-iii:
King Edward the Third is a history play from Shakespeare's age, credited in part to William Shakespeare. Its cast pairs the English court with the French. Edward the Third heads the list, with his son, the Prince of Wales. The earls of Warwick, Derby, and Salisbury stand among his lords.

Across the channel stand King John of France and his sons Charles and Philip. Queen Philippa and the Countess of Salisbury hold the women's parts. The scenes shift between England, Flanders, and France, following Edward's wars. The play also tells of Edward's siege of Calais and his love suit to the Countess. Scholars credit Shakespeare with the Countess scenes especially, among the finest in the play.
king-henry-viii:
William Shakespeare's King Henry VIII shows Queen Katherine near death in the passage sampled here. Katherine asks her listener to stand as friend to poor people. She begs him to urge the King to grant her last request. If heaven had given longer life, she says, they had not parted thus.

Katherine sends humble word that in death she blessed the King. Her eyes grow dim, and she calls for more women attendants. She asks to be strewn with maiden flowers after her death. Though unqueened, she wishes burial like a queen and king's daughter. The next act opens late at night with Bishop Gardiner and Sir Thomas Lovell.
king-richard-ii:
King Richard II, by William Shakespeare, opens as Richard calls on old John of Gaunt. Richard asks whether Gaunt has brought his bold son Henry here. Other nobles and attendants enter with the King and Gaunt. Henry Hereford must make good his late appeal in person. His charge is against Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, Richard says.

Gaunt answers simply that he has brought his son as asked. Richard then asks whether Gaunt has sounded Henry on his grounds. Does Henry act from ancient malice, Richard wants to know. Or does he charge Mowbray with known treachery, as subjects should? Gaunt replies that he sifted his son as near as possible.
king-richard-iii:
William Shakespeare's King Richard III is a history play about a ruthless royal villain. Richard, Duke of Gloucester, wants the English crown. He lies, plots, and murders his way toward it, even charming people he plans to harm.

Richard removes rivals one by one, including young princes held in the Tower. His rule brings fear rather than peace. At Bosworth Field his cause collapses, and he cries out for a horse. The role remains one of the great villain parts in drama. The play also shows how fear can hold a court together for a time. Richard's quick wit makes audiences follow him even while judging him.
lady-inger-of-ostrat-henrik-ibsen-s-pros:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Lady Inger of Ostrat in 1855, early in his career. Charles Archer translated this edition. It forms part of the third volume of Ibsen's prose dramas.

The action takes place at Ostrat Manor on the Trondheim fjord in 1528. Lady Inger, a widowed noblewoman, leads the cast. Her daughter Elina, a Danish knight, and Swedish soldiers surround her. Norway then lay under Danish power, and loyalties split every house. Ibsen turns that national struggle into a tense family and political drama. Archer's translation helped English readers meet Ibsen's early work. The play shows his later themes of duty and power already forming.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-ii:
Book Two of Lytton's Leila moves to the Christian army's camp. The Spanish king holds night counsel in his royal tent. A Dominican friar shares that tense scene.

A visitor and a hostage complicate the king's plans. Ambush, strife, and capture fill the chapters that follow. Leila's fate tightens as both camps claim her loyalty. Lytton keeps the siege of Granada as the great backdrop. Love, faith, and ambition collide under its walls in this middle book. Almamen the enchanter gives the tale a magical thread. Granada's palace scenes mix splendor with quiet dread.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-iii:
Book Three of Leila brings its heroine before the Inquisition. Torquemada's tribunal has summoned Leila from her fears. Her gentle nature ill fits her for such a contest, Lytton says.

Isabel, the Spanish queen, meets the Jewish maiden in chapter one. That meeting sets mercy against harsh religious power. Leila's father and lover pull her fate in opposed directions. The siege of Granada presses on outside the palace. Lytton's third book deepens the tale's religious and personal stakes. Almamen the enchanter gives the tale a magical thread. Granada's palace scenes mix splendor with quiet dread.
letters-of-horace-walpole-volume-ii:
Volume Two of Horace Walpole's letters covers 1764 to 1795. It opens with Madame de Boufflers visiting his house, Strawberry Hill. French opinions of the English character amuse him.

Letters treat debates on American taxes and Lord Byron's duel. One letter to Cole discusses his own novel, The Castle of Otranto. Almack's club, periwig makers, and ladies' head-dresses all get noticed. Walpole's pen turns high politics and fashion into comedy. These later letters show a master observer near the century's end. Later letters in this volume reach the 1760s. Strawberry Hill, his playful Gothic house, begins to rise in them.
ma-rkandeya-pura-na-books-vii-and-viii:
Books VII and VIII of the Mârkandeya Purâna appear here in English verse. The Reverend B. Hale Wortham translated them for the Royal Asiatic Society's Journal. That journal printed his work at London in 1881. The Purâna is one of Hinduism's great sacred story collections.

Book VII opens with the saintly King Harischandra on the throne. Under his rule no famine, pain, or untimely death touched his people. Hunting in the forest, he hears women crying out for help. Their plea sets his famous trials in motion. Wortham's rendering is among the first English versions of this text. It opens classical Hindu imagination to English readers.
memoirs-of-margaret-fuller-ossoli-volume:
Volume two of the Memoirs of Margaret Fuller Ossoli came out in Boston. Phillips, Sampson and Company printed it, with rights entered in 1851. The same Jonson and Leonardo lines head this volume as the first.

Part six, Jamaica Plain, is signed by W. H. Channing in the contents. First Impressions stands as a head under that part of the book. The memoirs gather her letters and the accounts of those who knew her. Two volumes were needed to hold a life cut short at its height. The contents run to part six, well past the mid point. Letters hold a large share of both volumes of her life.
nasa-tm-19640023768-preferred-parts-mech: Volume II of a NASA list of preferred mechanical parts for space vehicles is preserved here only as a garbled cover page. No author, center, or date can be read from the hosted sample. The title and catalog note alone identify its subject as the choice of reliable mechanical parts.
nasa-tm-19650006056-telemetry-instrument:
Harold S Horiuchi at Goddard Space Flight Center described the beacon telemetry gear flown on Echo II in October 1964. Echo II was a passive communications satellite, a large balloon that bounced radio signals back to Earth. It carried no active relay of its own.

Horiuchi covers the instruments that reported back on the satellite itself. Even a passive balloon needs a health signal so ground crews can track it. He presented the work at a military electronics meeting in Washington in September 1964. Readers see the small active system inside a mostly passive spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19650020080-epe-d-data-processin:
Marc Jay Selig prepared this data processing plan for the EPE-D mission, dated December 1, 1964, at Goddard. Volume II deals with the staff and organization behind the plan. EPE-D data from space flights had to be turned into usable records.

A processing plan assigns people, steps, and duties before data arrive. Volume II covers that human and office side, rather than circuits alone. Without such planning, flight data can pile up unread. The volume shows the office structure Goddard built to handle one mission's data flow from start to finish.
nasa-tm-19670015312-research-achievement:
The Research and Development Operations office at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, issued this volume in 1966. It is Volume II, Report Number 2, of the Research Achievements Review. This issue is devoted to thermophysics research at the center.

The review series covers fields such as radiation physics, atmospheric dynamics, instrumentation, and power systems. The catalog record lists this issue's topics in detail. They range from emissivity physics and thermal similitude to work on Pegasus satellite data. Ultraviolet effects on control surface materials and infrared instruments also appear. Each issue gathers work from across the center into one shared record.
nasa-tm-19670020052-research-achievement:
The Research and Development Operations office at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, issued this volume in 1966. It is Volume II, Report Number 4, of the Research Achievements Review, and the whole issue is devoted to materials research at the center. An introduction surveys the materials program before the individual studies begin.

One lead study, by Charles E. Cataldo, covers diffusion bonding of dissimilar metals, including joining methods, diffusion aids, and the bonding process itself. It reports mechanical test results and pressure tests on a twenty-inch diameter tank built by the method. The catalog record lists the issue's other topics: stress corrosion tests, nondestructive testing methods, material designs for electronic equipment, and development of nonmetallic materials. Together the pieces show how Marshall attacked the material problems of large launch vehicles.
on-the-seashore-cassell-s-eyes-and-no-ey:
R. Cadwallader Smith wrote this nature book for children. It is book seven in Cassell's Eyes and No Eyes series. Eight color plates and many drawings fill the book. Lesson one meets a shore creature called Five-Fingered Jack. Later lessons stroll the shore and watch its birds.

Crabs, shrimps, prawns, and barnacles each get a lesson. Shore plants, seaweeds, and jellyfish follow in turn. Two lessons treat shells and the animals that build them. Smith teaches children to look closely at common things. The series name promises eyes opened to nature. It suits young readers who love the beach.
pamela-volume-ii:
Volume Two of Richardson's Pamela continues the heroine's letters after her marriage. Richardson's own preface, written as the Editor, opens it. The first part, he boasts, succeeded beyond his most sanguine expectations. He hopes these letters are equally written to nature. No romantic nights, improbable surprises, or irrational machinery appear. New and practicable rules for the conduct of life run throughout.

Pamela now shines in an exalted condition. She is an affectionate wife and a faithful friend. A polite neighbor, an indulgent mother, and a beneficent mistress follow. The Editor confesses his real difficulty was selection. Married life with Mr. and Mrs. B. supplied too much material. He also hints the story has a foundation in truth. Names and circumstances were disguised for obvious reasons.
podcast-dannyjones-_7IWPfhE4II:
Ian Carroll joins Danny Jones for a dark tour of power inside the Vatican. The episode title names evil in the church, Satan worship, and a spy war few people talk about. Carroll is known for digging into hidden networks.

Carroll lays out his claims about secret deals, hidden money, and spies who work the halls of the church. He ties old scandals to spies and states that used the church for cover. Jones asks where the proof ends and the guesswork starts. Listeners get a tense, shadow filled talk on faith and power. The library files it as an archive record, without a side taken.
podcast-joerogan-O1B44VmZFiI:
Dr. Shanna Swan tells Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, how plastics in food may be harming our hormones. Swan is an epidemiologist who studies how chemicals in daily products affect fertility. Her research has drawn wide attention and real alarm.

She explains how compounds that leak from packaging can mimic hormones in the body, and what her studies link them to, from sperm counts to early development. Rogan asks what a person can actually change at home. The segment is a clear statement of a serious public-health warning, from the scientist most tied to it.
podcast-tuckercarlson-JGchqvMtvII:
Tucker Carlson confronts the head of a biotechnology company in this episode. He presses him over genetic alteration of the next generation. The subjects include embryos edited, traits selected, and a future in which children are designed. Carlson frames the technology as a moral emergency, and the executive must answer for his industry's direction.

The confrontation format serves Carlson's argument that biotech advances by euphemism, calling redesign by softer names. His guest defends the work in the language of health and choice. Between them sits the genuine question the episode, whatever its staging, does raise: who decides what may be changed in a human being before birth. The recording preserves a rare direct clash between a populist broadcaster and the industry he accuses, unmediated by a panel or a moderator.
podcast-tuckercarlson-vydAb4RR1iI:
Tucker Carlson and budget chief Russ Vought break down the DOGE project and Trump's cabinet picks in this episode. Vought, an architect of the administration's plans, gives an insider's guide to the new team. The hour is wonky by design, naming names and roles.

Vought explains what the cost-cutting effort aims to do inside federal agencies. He and Carlson grade the cabinet choices made so far, post by post. They discuss which picks will fight the bureaucracy and which may fold. Political and curious viewers get a clear map of who holds power and why it matters.
poems-by-jean-ingelow-in-two-volumes-vol:
Jean Ingelow's Poems conclude in this second volume of the author's complete edition, published in Boston by Roberts Brothers in 1896. An illustration shows her former home in Boston, Lincolnshire, with St. Botolph's Church in the distance, tying the poet to the flat fen country that shaped her imagination. The volume opens with a tribute poem by Susan Coolidge, picturing Ingelow singing first in youth and then again with trained voice and ripened art.

Coolidge recalls the Songs of Seven, Ingelow's early triumph, and urges the singer to sing on until earth greets heaven. The poems that follow complete the gathering Ingelow herself approved, the second half of a two-volume life's work. For readers who know her through anthologies, the complete edition shows the full range: narrative, lyric, and devotional verse from one of Victorian England's best-selling poets.
queechy-volume-ii: Queechy, volume two, completes the Tauchnitz edition of Elizabeth Wetherell's novel, issued at Leipzig as volume 312 of the Collection of British Authors in 1854. Only the title pages are shown. They present the second tome of the two-volume set. The author's name is given as the author of The Wide, Wide World. The same Tauchnitz list of her other books appears. It names The Hills of the Shatemuc. It names Say and Seal and The Old Helmet.
roman-history-books-i-iii:
Titus Livius, in Livy's Roman history, is translated here by John Henry Freese, Alfred John Church, and William Jackson Brodribb. Duffield Osborne supplies a critical and biographical introduction and notes, in an illustrated edition dated 1904. His introduction begins with regret for the lost books of Livy.

The whole work filled one hundred and forty-two books, Osborne writes, carrying Rome's story from Aeneas to the death of Drusus in 9 B.C. Only parts survive, the first ten books among them, telling of early Rome to 294 B.C. This volume holds the opening books of that surviving history, in which Rome rises from a city to the ruling power in Italy.
royalty-restored-or-london-under-charles:
J. Fitzgerald Molloy wrote Royalty Restored, or London Under Charles II, and gave the book to Thomas Hardy with thanks owed, he says, by all readers of English. In his preface to the first edition Molloy claims that no social history of the court of Charles II had yet been written. The Grammont Memoirs, he argues, lack date and detail and speak only to readers out for amusement. They give brief, faulty sketches of the wits and beauties who crowded the court of the merry monarch while the French writer stayed in England.

Pepys and Evelyn, the other chief witnesses, also fall short for Molloy's purpose. Pepys, across the first nine years of the Restoration, passes on such gossip about Whitehall as reached him. Evelyn records some small acts of the king and his courtiers, more to point a moral than to adorn a tale.
sir-george-tressady-volume-ii:
Mrs. Humphry Ward carries her political novel into volume two, opening at Part Two, chapter thirteen. A hot June morning finds George Tressady walking from Brook Street to Warwick Square, four weeks after a Castle Luton visit. He seeks his mother's signature on a paper tied to the Shapetsky talks, then plans the House of Commons.

Her drawing room, crowded with notes, bills, draper's patterns, and flattering portraits, irks him even as he owns his own room matches it. A scene with his mother may await, and Letty's excuses press on him. Public duty and private strain tighten together.
the-autobiography-of-a-journalist-volume:
Volume two of William James Stillman's life story, dated 1901, picks up with consular life in Crete. Chapters follow an insurrection there, diplomacy, and time in Athens. Stillman then writes about Rossetti and his friends before returning to journalism.

War reporting fills much of the later contents. Headings name Montenegro and its prince, revolt in Herzegovina, a trip across Montenegro and Albania, and work at Ragusa. The war of 1876 and Russian action in 1877 lead to the taking of Niksich and Moratsha. A final group returns to the Levant, Greek quarrels, Florence, and a blockade of Greece.
the-autobiography-of-a-play-papers-on-pl:
Bronson Howard's lecture, issued in 1914 for the Dramatic Museum of Columbia University, forms the second part of Papers on Play-Making. Augustus Thomas supplied an introduction. Howard read the piece before the Shakspere Club of Harvard University.

Howard tells students he will not lecture on Greek drama or the old unities, except where they bear on craft. He credits Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides with teaching later writers how plays are built. Yet he argues that the laws behind drama lie in human feeling itself. They waited, like laws of nature, to be found and used by working playwrights.
the-bostonians-vol-ii-of-ii:
Henry James wrote The Bostonians, a novel first put out in 1886. Volume II came out in London from Macmillan and Company in 1921. It picks the tale up at chapter twenty-four, in the second book. The scene is Doctor Tarrant's house at Monadnoc Place,.

Basil Ransom has come to call and waits in the parlour for Miss Tarrant. A young maid lets the ladies know he is there, but no one comes down at once. Ransom takes up the one book on the table. It is a life of Mrs. Ada T. P. Foat, the famed trance speaker, with a portrait of her in ringlets. He reads a few pages, mocks it as North writing, and tosses it back. The bare, hot, poor room draws his eye while he waits, though he is a man who notes how folk live only when a room is fine.
the-decameron-volume-ii: Volume II of Giovanni Boccaccio's Decameron, faithfully translated by J. M. Rigg with illustrations by Louis Chalon, is shown here through the contents of the Fifth Day. The summaries promise tales of lovers parted and rejoined: Cimon, made wise by love, wins Iphigenia by capture on the high seas. Gostanza, thinking Martuccio dead, sets out alone by boat and finds him alive in Tunis. Pietro Boccamazza flees with Agnolella and escapes robbers before their marriage in Rome. Only the title page and these day-five summaries are present here.
the-dramatic-works-of-gerhart-hauptmann-: Volume two of The Dramatic Works of Gerhart Hauptmann, a 1913 authorized edition edited by Ludwig Lewisohn, holds three social dramas in his English versions. They are Drayman Henschel, Rose Bernd, and The Rats. The first play's cast list names Henschel, his wife, and Hanne Schäl. It also names Bertha and horse dealer Walther. Only the title matter, contents, and that cast list are present here.
the-guide-to-reading-the-pocket-universi:
Lyman Abbott, Asa Don Dickinson, and others edited The Guide to Reading. It is Volume XXIII of The Pocket University. A contents list names the parts. Books for Study and Reading is by Abbott. John Macy contributes The Purpose of Reading. From Richard Le Gallienne comes How to Get the Best Out of Books. Dickinson supplies The Guide to Daily Reading.

Abbott's opening essay gives books three uses in a house: they can serve as ornaments, as tools, or as friends. For the first he tells of a millionaire building a fourth house by the sea.
