A house ought to have a library, so one was built. When the house was finished, the library shelves proved too shallow for books of ordinary size. The millionaire refused to alter them. He told the architect to purchase handsome bindings of the classics and fasten them into the shelves with glue.
the-house-of-pride-and-other-tales-of-ha:
Jack London set the stories in this collection in Hawaii. The text follows the 1919 Mills and Boon edition. The contents list six tales. They include Koolau the Leper and Good-bye, Jack. Aloha Oe and Chun Ah Chun follow. The Sheriff of Kona completes the list. The title story opens at a farewell ball. Officers of the Twentieth are leaving Honolulu for Alaska. Percival Ford attends, though he did not want to come.

Ford does not dance. He does not care for army people. His wealth and standing still make his presence unavoidable. He leads much of Hawaii's commercial life. London draws him as fastidious and ill at ease. Bare-shouldered women and hard-drinking officers jar him. He prefers the committee women who seek his advice. They come to him for contributions as well. The portrait sets island pride up for a fall. The title promises exactly that.
the-last-days-of-pompeii:
Edward George Bulwer-Lytton sets his novel in Pompeii before the eruption that buried the city. Book one opens with Clodius and the portly Diomed trading talk on the street. Both men discuss supping with Glaucus, whose dinners draw praise even when his wine runs short.

Talk turns to dice, wealth, and pleasure, and Diomed boasts of his wine cellars and fish ponds. The light street scene carries a dark edge for readers who know the city fate. Bulwer-Lytton fills Roman daily life with talk, baths, temples, and display in homes, streets, and temples across the wealthy resort city.
the-life-and-letters-of-walter-h-page-vo: Burton J. Hendrick wrote the life and letters of Walter H. Page, and volume two appeared at Garden City, New York, in 1924. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing chapters from the Lusitania sinking through dark days for the Allies, the Balfour mission, and getting American troops to France. A closing chapter on Page as a man and an appendix follow the war chapters. The letters and narrative themselves are missing from this record.
the-life-and-voyages-of-christopher-colu: Washington Irving wrote his life and voyages of Christopher Columbus, and volume two of his revised edition appeared in 1892. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, listing book eleven chapters on the Adelantado administration, tribute at Xaragua, Roldan conspiracy, and Guarionex insurrections. Book twelve opens with confusion in the island and talks with rebels. The narrative itself is not included in this record beyond those headings.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-02:
Part two of Motley's historical introduction argues that five centuries of isolation followed Rome's fall in the Netherlands as across Europe. A thousand obscure streams slowly prepared a great river of culture through dismal centuries of feudalism with little talk of human right.

Three great forces then arise and act on each other and on society. First comes the sword, the force of iron, as a land's master holds territory and people and grants portions to subalterns in return for faithful swords, with vassals subdividing further. Feudal power thus becomes the ground from which Dutch liberty must grow.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-11:
Motley's record for the second part of 1566 is headed in its own pages as volume twelve, although the record title calls it volume eleven, and readers should note that numbering clash. Its chapter eight summary covers secret policy, envoys in Spain, debates at Segovia, and the Duchess's correspondence with Philip.

Margaret misrepresents Orange, Egmont, and others while praising them in friendly letters, and Philip answers with wrath and duplicity. Egmont labors in Flanders and Orange keeps Antwerp tolerant. The same chapter summary opens the complete portion for 1566 to 1574 in the set, and readers should expect overlapping text there.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-13:
Headed volume fourteen in its own pages, this portion opens Alva's chapter. The record title calls it volume thirteen instead. Cabinet quarrels fill the summary's opening lines here. Ruy Gomez and Alva contend in the Spanish cabinet. The Netherlands conquest goes to Alva at last. His birth, career, and character receive a sketch. His invading army organizes and marches to the provinces.

Margaret complains as Alva demands city keys. Garrisons enter the great cities under his orders. Secret plans already fix the coming arrests. Orange, Egmont, and Horn all stand named for seizure. Egmont ignores warnings from friends like De Billy. He walks toward the trap with strange infatuation. Invasion works by paperwork and banquets here. Soldiers play only a supporting part in it.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-15:
Headed volume sixteen in its own pages, though the record calls it volume fifteen, this portion covers 1568 in chapter three. Alva moves into Friesland against Count Louis, whose troops mutiny near Jemmingen before artful strategy destroys his army and Spanish outrages follow.

A long episode then weighs fables about Don Carlos and Queen Isabella, Philip's secret letters to the Pope, and testimony for and against the king from envoys and historians. Battle narrative gives way to a court mystery that Motley refuses to settle cheaply. Utrecht also sees an execution in the summary's sweep.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-25:
Headed volume twenty-seven in its own pages, though the record calls it volume twenty-five, this portion covers 1577 in chapter two. Don John enters Brussels in triumph, then secret letters with Escovedo and Antonio Perez expose plots, despondency, and calls for severe measures.

Orange's toleration toward Catholics and Anabaptists draws censure even from friends, Viglius dies, envoys meet at Gertruydenberg without result, and a man named Peter Panis is executed for heresy. Three parties divide the provinces while the governor dissembles and dreads capture. Triumph curdles quickly in Motley's telling.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-26:
Headed volume twenty-eight in its own pages, though the record calls it volume twenty-six, this portion covers 1577 in chapter three. Margaret of Valois intrigues in Hainault for Alencon and is feasted by Don John at Namur, after which the governor seizes Namur's citadel and plans Antwerp's.

An attempt on Antwerp's citadel fails through a fortunate panic among German mercenaries, foreign troops evacuate the city, intercepted letters expose the governor's private schemes, and Orange tours Holland and Utrecht. Festivity, seizure, and exposure follow in quick order, leaving trust in ruins.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-28:
Headed volume thirty in its own pages, though the record calls it volume twenty-eight, this portion covers 1578 in chapter five. Don John takes towns, Amsterdam attempts and accepts a satisfaction, royal letters arrive through De Selles, and correspondence flies between king, governor, and States-General.

New forces gather, Amsterdam undergoes a municipal revolution, and Orange writes on the Anabaptists of Middelburg while armies idle. John Casimir and Alencon enter the tangle, with Elizabeth's perverse politics angering all sides. Foreign patrons multiply far faster than victories in this crowded, tangled year of war.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-29:
Headed volume thirty-one in its own pages, though the record calls it volume twenty-nine, this portion opens part six on Alexander of Parma for 1578 to 1584. Farnese's birth, education, marriage, exploits at Lepanto and Gembloux, appearance, and character introduce the new governor.

Anjou at Mons, Casimir intriguing at Ghent, foreign troops ravaging the provinces, riots and image-breaking, and Orange establishing a religious peace at Ghent fill the summary. Elizabeth rebukes Casimir sharply before he departs. A gifted new Spanish commander inherits a Netherlands bitterly at war with itself.
the-wonders-of-pompeii: Marc Monnier's The Wonders of Pompeii reached English readers in Charles Scribner and Company's 1871 edition. The title page notes a translation from the original French. No translator is named on the pages shown. An illustration shows excavations directed by Inspector Fiorelli in 1860. The book belonged to an Illustrated Library of Wonders series. Companion volumes covered optics, heat, and glass-making.
the-works-of-aphra-behn-volume-ii:
Montague Summers edited volume two of The Works of Aphra Behn, gathering four plays and notes. Abdelazer, The City Heiress, and The Feign'd Curtezans are included. The Young King completes the set. A plot summary opens Abdelazer, the Moor's revenge tragedy. Spain's old king conquered Fez and killed its monarch. He then raised the orphaned prince Abdelazer as his general.

Abdelazer burns for revenge rather than love. He becomes the Queen's lover to gain influence. Together they poison the King. Accusations of adultery and murder follow at court. Behn's drama mixes lust, ambition, and violence freely. Readers meet Restoration theatre at its most sensational.
the-works-of-aphra-behn-volume-iii:
Volume three of The Works of Aphra Behn, edited by Montague Summers, appeared in 1915. Five plays fill the volume, followed by notes. They include The Town-Fop, The False Count, and The Lucky Chance. The Forc'd Marriage and The Emperor of the Moon complete the list. A plot summary introduces The Town-Fop first.

Sir Timothy Tawdrey is promised to Celinda by family arrangement. Celinda instead loves Bellmour, Lord Plotwell's nephew. Sir Timothy challenges his rival but fails to appear for the duel. Bellmour is secretly admitted to Celinda's chamber at night. Her brother surprises them yet favors the match. Behn's comedies turn on wit, disguise, and forced marriages.
tieck-the-rebellion-in-the-cevennes-vol-:
French Protestants in the Cevennes mountains rose against Louis the Fourteenth's persecution in the early 1700s, and Tieck turned their revolt into a historical novel. The Rebellion in the Cevennes, Volume Two, appears here in English. The Camisard rebels, peasants and prophets, fight a king's army for their faith.

Tieck treats the rebels with Romantic sympathy, finding epic courage in desperate people. Prophecy, ambush, and betrayal drive the closing volume toward its grim reckoning. Religious war becomes human drama rather than polemic in his hands. English readers meet a little-known side of German fiction: the historical novel of faith under fire. The mountains themselves brood over every chapter.
to-the-gold-coast-for-gold-a-personal-na: Volume two of Richard F. Burton and Verney Lovett Cameron's Gold Coast narrative continues the contents from chapter twelve. Headings follow the Sierra Leonean at home and abroad, then travel from Sierra Leone to Cape Palmas and Axim. Later chapters visit concessions at Apatim, Izrah, and Inyoko, meet King Blay, and reach mines at Abosu and Takwa. A conclusion follows the return to Axim and departure for Europe. A contents list alone is on these pages, so the narrative itself is not shown.
two-years-ago-volume-ii:
Volume two of Charles Kingsley's Two Years Ago, in the same 1901 printing, carries the novel from chapter fifteen to chapter twenty-eight. The contents promise the cruise of the Waterwitch, a black hound, Beddgelert, and Baalzebub's banquet. The banker's daughter, an explosion in an ancient crater, and last Christmas Eve close the list.

Chapter fifteen opens in mid-August, with Aberalva awaiting the homecoming of Frederick Viscount Scoutbush. Flags deck the shipping and Sunday clothes come out for the day. Elsley, his brother-in-law, has made up his mind to the visit with stately sulkiness. The village's awful jubilation sets the volume's social comedy moving.
un-doc-united-nations-special-committee-:
Chapter II of the 1947 report of the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine sets out the background to the Palestine question. The committee, known as UNSCOP, was sent to study the land after Britain said it would give up its mandate there. Eleven states sat on the panel.

The chapter reviews the land's recent past, its peoples, and the rival claims to it. It covers the mandate years, Jewish immigration, and Arab resistance in plain factual terms. Later chapters build their plans on this base. The chapter is the factual spine of a famous report.

Final advice to the General Assembly fills Chapter VII of the 1947 report of the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine. After months of hearings and travel, the panel had to state what it advised. Its members did not agree, so the report closes with rival plans side by side.

The majority plan backs partition into two states joined in an economic union. The minority plan backs one federal state shared by both peoples. The chapter states both cases fairly and in full. It is the last word of a report that helped set the course of the region.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Annex II to General Assembly Resolution 13, from 1946, holds the provisional staff regulations for the United Nations Secretariat. The rules define staff as international civil servants. They serve the Organization alone and take no orders from any government. Before starting work, they swear an oath of loyalty, care, and secrecy.

Later sections cover hiring on merit, with men and women equally eligible. They also cover probation, training, and promotion. Other sections cover pay, hours, leave, and discipline. The rules set the normal retirement age at sixty. They allow dismissal for poor service or serious misconduct. They also provide travel costs, a staff provident fund, and payment for staff hurt on duty.
un-un-res-united-nations-special-committ:
Chapter II of the report of the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine lays out the facts behind the Palestine question, as the panel found them in 1947. The committee, UNSCOP, was charged with studying the mandate's future after Britain decided to hand the problem to the UN. This chapter is its factual base.

The chapter reviews the land, its two peoples, and the history of the mandate since the First World War. It sets out Jewish and Arab claims side by side. Later chapters argue over plans, but this one sticks to the record. It remains a clear primer on the dispute.
unspoken-sermons-series-i-ii-and-iii: George MacDonald gathered his Unspoken Sermons in three series, bound here in one volume. The pages here give the title page and contents only, so the sermons themselves do not appear. Titles from the first series include The Child in the Midst, The Consuming Fire, and The Higher Faith. Two more name the duties of love: Love Thy Neighbour and Love Thine Enemy. The second series adds The Way, The Word of Jesus on Prayer, and Self-Denial.
vixen-volume-ii: Volume two of M. E. Braddon's Vixen forms volume 1810 of the Tauchnitz Collection of British Authors, printed at Leipzig by Bernhard Tauchnitz in 1879, with the right of translation reserved. Pages present here hold the series title pages and the heading of a contents list for the volume, with no entries under it, so the story itself is not shown. Braddon is billed as the author of Lady Audley's Secret. The middle volume of her three-volume novel thus stands here as a frame without its chapters.

voltaire-history-charles-xii:
Voltaire published his History of Charles XII, King of Sweden, in 1731, early in his path to fame. Charles was the warrior king whose campaigns shook the north of Europe in his youth. Voltaire, still in his thirties, turned that life into a new kind of history: swift, clear, and built like a story.

The book follows Charles from boy king to invader of Russia, and on to his fall and death in Norway. Voltaire writes of war's glory and waste in the same cool voice. His Charles is brave past reason, a hero who ruins his own kingdom. The work became the model for the modern historical life, read across Europe.
we-and-the-world-a-book-for-boys-part-ii:
Part two of Juliana Horatia Ewing's We and the World, a book for boys, takes her young narrator out into the world at last. Chapter one bears an old proverb for its motto, about a friend in need. The boy counts his biggest stroke of luck at the outset, luck he did not know he had. The man he sat beside in the railway carriage was not a rogue.

He travelled third class to Liverpool, he says, partly because it was cheapest, and partly to dodge family friends. His seatmate, a third-class passenger bound the same way, somehow guessed three things. The boy was running away. He carried money. He had never seen Liverpool. This second part shares its title page house, the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, with the first. It carries the runaway to sea.
within-the-deep-cassell-s-eyes-and-no-ey:
R. Cadwallader Smith wrote this sea nature book for children. It is Book VIII in Cassell's Eyes and No Eyes series. The contents promise lessons on flat fish, seals, whales, and strange nurseries. Later lessons cover rock-pool fish, curious fishes, and a garden of the sea. Eight colour plates support the lessons.

Lesson one begins with the herring. Smith calls it the fish that most deserves attention in the wide ocean world. Young readers learn to look closely at common sea life. Each lesson mixes simple facts with wonder at size, danger, and odd habits.
